entities.summary:
The Democratic Party of the United States, one of the world's two oldest continuously operating political parties (founded 1828 from the Democratic-Republican Party under Andrew Jackson), is a center-left party that has governed America through the Civil War era (as the party of the Confederacy), the Progressive Era (Wilson), the New Deal (Roosevelt), the Great Society (Johnson), and now progressive social liberalism under Biden. The Democratic Party's ideological transformation from the party of slavery and Jim Crow to the party of civil rights between 1860 and 1968 is the most dramatic political realignment in American history.

Andrew Jackson's 1828 presidential campaign established the Democratic Party as the party of the 'common man' against the Whig establishment — using mass campaign techniques, popular rallies, and direct voter mobilization that established American mass democracy. Through the 19th century, Democrats dominated Southern politics, defending slavery, then Reconstruction resistance, then Jim Crow segregation. Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal (1933-1940) transformed the party into a coalition of labor, minorities, Catholics, Jews, and Southern whites.

The decisive realignment came with Lyndon Johnson's Civil Rights Act (1964) and Voting Rights Act (1965), which transferred Black voters to the Democrats and white Southerners to the Republicans — completing the 'Southern Strategy' switch. Today's Democratic Party spans corporate centrists (Biden, Clinton), democratic socialists (Sanders, AOC), and civil rights progressives. The party's dilemma — holding together urban progressives, suburban moderates, and rural working-class voters — defines American political competition in the 21st century.
